title: How to pick a ripe avocado
summary: An underripe avocado is hard and astringent; an overripe one turns stringy and bitter, and either will ruin the dish you…
body_text:
An underripe avocado is hard and astringent; an overripe one turns stringy and bitter, and either will ruin the dish you bought it for. The most reliable test is not the colour of the skin — it is pressing gently around the stem with your fingertips.

## Judging by feel

An unripe avocado barely yields at all; the skin feels as hard as a stone. One at its peak gives a slight, even depression when cradled in your palm and squeezed gently, then springs back slowly. If it sinks deep without recovering, or feels loose and watery, it has almost certainly gone past its best.

## The stem test

Flick off the small stem cap at the top of the fruit. Bright green underneath means it needs a few more days. Pale brown usually means it is exactly ready. Dark brown or black generally means it is overripe, or has started to blacken inside.

## Ripening and storage

An unripe avocado can be ripened faster by leaving it in a paper bag with an apple or a banana at room temperature — usually one to three days. One that is already ripe but not wanted yet should go in the fridge, which will slow further softening for another two or three days.

title: Growing tomatoes on a balcony
summary: The most common reason balcony tomatoes fail is not the wrong variety — it is too little sun and too small a pot. Tomato…
body_text:
The most common reason balcony tomatoes fail is not the wrong variety — it is too little sun and too small a pot. Tomatoes are sun-lovers, needing at least six hours of direct light a day before they will flower and set fruit, and no amount of feeding will make up for a shaded balcony.

## Pots and growing medium

For a home balcony, choose a small-fruited or cherry variety; the root system is more modest and suits a ten to fifteen litre pot. Use a peat-based mix with perlite for drainage. Waterlogging at the bottom of the pot, and the root rot that follows, is what kills more balcony tomatoes than anything else.

## Watering rhythm

Tomatoes dislike swinging between bone dry and soaking. Let the surface of the soil dry, then water thoroughly. During fruiting this matters most: erratic watering is what splits the fruit. Watering early in the morning beats watering at dusk, as it leaves less overnight humidity for disease to take hold in.

## Staking and side shoots

Stake the plant once it reaches about thirty centimetres, before the weight of fruit can snap a stem. Tomatoes throw out side shoots from every leaf axil continuously; unless you deliberately want a bushier plant carrying more but smaller fruit, pinch them out regularly so the plant's energy goes into the main stem and the fruit it is already carrying.

title: Common pests and diseases on balcony tomatoes
summary: Balcony tomatoes are spared the large-scale disease pressure of a field, but poor airflow and pots packed closely togeth…
headings: Aphids and whitefly on leaf undersides
body_text:
Balcony tomatoes are spared the large-scale disease pressure of a field, but poor airflow and pots packed closely together still bring a predictable handful of problems. Caught early, most of them can be handled without reaching for chemicals — there is no need to wait until a whole plant is dying.

## Aphids and whitefly on leaf undersides

Clusters of small insects on new growth and the undersides of leaves are usually aphids or whitefly. They feed on sap and excrete a sticky residue that invites sooty mould. A few can be rubbed off by hand or blasted with a jet of water; larger infestations respond to diluted soap spray applied over three to five consecutive days, avoiding the hottest part of the afternoon.

## Leaf spot and early blight

Brown concentric rings on the lower leaves, spreading as the leaf yellows and drops, is typically early blight, and it thrives in long spells of humid, still weather. Pick off and dispose of affected leaves immediately rather than letting them lie on the soil surface, and open up the spacing between plants so foliage is not staying wet for hours at a time.

## Suffocated roots

If a plant is visibly stalled and the lower leaves are yellowing with no sign of insects, check the drainage holes at the base of the pot first. Oxygen starvation at the roots looks remarkably like a nutrient deficiency from the outside, and reaching for fertiliser will make it worse rather than better.

title: Bike chain care and when to replace it
summary: The chain is the fastest-wearing part of a bicycle drivetrain and the one whose maintenance is most often neglected. A w…
headings: How often to lubricate, and how
body_text:
The chain is the fastest-wearing part of a bicycle drivetrain and the one whose maintenance is most often neglected. A well-cared-for chain can cover several thousand kilometres; a neglected one can start to stretch and deform in under half that, taking an expensive cassette and chainrings down with it.

## How often to lubricate, and how

For ordinary commuting, lubricate every two to three hundred kilometres, and more often if you regularly ride in the rain or through standing water. Wipe the old oil and grit off the chain with a dry rag first. After applying lubricant, leave it a few minutes to work into the rollers, then wipe the excess off the outside — oil left on the surface simply collects dust and turns into grinding paste.

## Knowing when to replace it

The usual method is a chain wear gauge, which tells you whether the chain has stretched beyond a safe limit. A chain left on too long has a lengthened pitch that chews through the cassette's tooth profile, and once the cassette has to be replaced alongside it the repair costs several times more.

## Cleaning and storage

Before a long spell off the bike, clean the chain thoroughly and lubricate it, which greatly reduces the chance of surface rust while it sits. If you do not wipe the chain down after a wet ride, grit works its way between the rollers and the side plates — and it is those fine particles, rather than the water itself, that actually accelerate chain wear.

title: What to watch for when trimming a cat's claws
summary: Overgrown claws snag on fabric and furniture and can injure the cat, and they make an ordinary scratch far more likely t…
headings: If you cut too far and it bleeds
body_text:
Overgrown claws snag on fabric and furniture and can injure the cat, and they make an ordinary scratch far more likely to break skin. Regular trimming is basic home care. But a cat's claw is built differently from a dog's, and cutting in the wrong place draws blood easily — which is usually enough to make the cat resist every attempt afterwards.

## Understanding the structure

Hold a claw up to the light and you can see a pink wedge inside it — the quick, which carries blood and nerves. Trimming must stay well clear of it, taking only the clear or white tip. Dark claws do not show the quick, and there the safest approach is to take a very small amount at a time, across several sessions, rather than risk one deep cut.

## Settling the cat first

Most cats dislike having a paw held still, and grabbing one suddenly to start cutting almost guarantees a struggle. Start when the cat is relaxed or half asleep, pressing the pad gently so the claw extends on its own, and let it get used to having its paws handled before any trimming happens.

## If you cut too far and it bleeds

If you do catch the quick, stay calm. Pressing styptic powder or plain cornflour against the tip for a minute or two will normally stop the bleeding. With neither to hand, pressing the claw into a clean bar of soap works much the same way. Afterwards, slow down and take less off each time, so the next session is less likely to end the same way.

title: How to store beans for pour-over coffee
summary: Coffee beans begin oxidising slowly the moment roasting finishes, and how they are stored often affects the cup more tha…
body_text:
Coffee beans begin oxidising slowly the moment roasting finishes, and how they are stored often affects the cup more than the difference in quality between the beans you bought. When people find their coffee has gone flat, storage is usually the culprit rather than stale beans.

## The four enemies

Light, air, moisture and heat are what degrade beans fastest. A clear jar on a sunny windowsill looks lovely and is the quickest way to strip the aroma out of what is inside it. A poorly sealed zip bag is barely better, leaving the beans in continuous contact with the oxygen and humidity of the room.

## Choosing a container

An opaque, airtight canister with a one-way valve is the accepted best option: it lets the carbon dioxide that freshly roasted beans give off escape, while keeping outside air out. Failing that, decant into opaque sealed bags and press as much air out of each one as you can before closing it.

## Whether to freeze

Beans you will finish within a week or two need nothing more than an airtight container somewhere cool and dark. Moving them in and out of the fridge repeatedly is actively harmful, as the temperature swing condenses moisture on the surface of the beans. If you have bought more than you can drink soon, divide them into small portions and freeze those — and once a portion comes out, use it rather than refreezing it.

title: A half-day walking route through Dadaocheng, Taipei
summary: Dadaocheng is one of the few districts in Taipei where the old street fabric survives more or less intact. It rewards an…
headings: Morning: the southern end of Dihua Street
Afternoon: the wharf and the sunset
body_text:
Dadaocheng is one of the few districts in Taipei where the old street fabric survives more or less intact. It rewards an unhurried half-day on foot, with the emphasis on the buildings and the feel of the streets rather than on covering as many sights as possible.

## Morning: the southern end of Dihua Street

Start from Beimen station and walk north along Dihua Street. The southern stretch is dominated by dried-goods sellers and traditional pharmacies, and the Baroque facades above the arcades are what deserve a slow pace here — many of the signs and mouldings are original rather than later reproductions.

## Midday: food around Yongle Market

The lanes around Yongle Market hold a good number of long-established food stalls. They are busiest at conventional mealtimes, so arriving half an hour early or late makes it considerably easier to find a seat and avoids the worst of the queues.

## Afternoon: the wharf and the sunset

Follow Minsheng West Road down to the Tamsui riverside. Dadaocheng Wharf is a popular spot to watch the sun go down, with a cycle path and seating along the bank. Late in the day the light on the water against the ridgeline of Guanyin Mountain opposite makes this the part of the route most worth lingering over.

title: Maintaining a home dehumidifier
summary: When a dehumidifier's output drops noticeably after a full damp season, the compressor is rarely the problem. Far more o…
headings: How often to clean the filter
body_text:
When a dehumidifier's output drops noticeably after a full damp season, the compressor is rarely the problem. Far more often it is a filter and a water tank that have gone months without cleaning. Routine maintenance takes about ten minutes and adds substantially to the life of the machine.

## How often to clean the filter

The filter catches dust from the incoming air and should be vacuumed or rinsed every two weeks. Near a busy road, or in a home with pets, weekly is better. A clogged filter does not only reduce output — over time it also forces the compressor to work harder than it was designed to.

## The tank and mould

The water tank is where mould establishes itself most readily, particularly if the machine runs for over a week without being emptied. Empty and rinse it daily, and once a month scrub it thoroughly with a diluted neutral detergent to stop a slimy film of scale building up.

## Where to put it

Leave at least twenty centimetres between the air outlet and any wall, or the machine simply draws its own damp exhaust back in and the middle of the room never dries out. Avoid running it inside a closed cabinet as well: poor heat dissipation shortens the compressor's life.

title: How water temperature and grind size interact in pour-over
summary: The same beans, brewed at a different temperature or ground a little coarser, can taste like two entirely different coff…
body_text:
The same beans, brewed at a different temperature or ground a little coarser, can taste like two entirely different coffees. Temperature and grind are not two knobs to be set independently; they have to be matched to each other before a brew becomes repeatable.

## What temperature changes

Hotter water extracts faster, drawing out more acidity and aroma — but past a point it also pulls harsh and astringent flavours along with them. Light roasts usually need the higher end (around 92 to 96°C) to open up fully. Dark roasts give up their solubles much more readily, and at high temperatures they simply turn bitter, so somewhere around 85 to 90°C suits them better.

## How grind size fits in

A finer grind means more surface area in contact with the water and therefore faster extraction; a coarser grind does the reverse. Run hot water through a fine grind and the two accelerating factors compound, which is a reliable way to over-extract into bitterness and astringency. Go the other way — cool water through a coarse grind — and you under-extract, leaving something thin and sour.

## Deciding what to change

If the cup is bitter and drying, reach first for a coarser grind or a lower temperature. If it is sour and thin, do the opposite: grind finer or raise the temperature. Change one variable at a time, or you will not be able to tell which one actually moved the flavour.
